title: Solar photovoltaic scale-up from expensive deployment to rapidly falling installed system costs
pressure: PV was technically established but expensive at installed-system scale; module production, balance-of-system cost, finance, deployment practice and policy all constrained diffusion.
preExistingWorldModel: Laboratory efficiency and commercial modules existed; policy incentives and manufacturing learning were already recognized as important but costs remained high.
candidateRoutes: manufacturing scale and module cost reduction
observationsAndInstruments: NREL/LBNL price tracking documented rapid installed-price decline through 2012-2014.
A 2014 NREL benchmark found modeled residential cash-purchase price 46% below its inflation-adjusted Q4 2010 benchmark and attributed recent decline substantially to global module price reductions.
Historical price work distinguishes module-cost decline from persistent non-module/soft costs.
decisiveTests: installed system price rather than cell efficiency alone
technicalOrScientificTransition: PV moved from a technically valid generation route toward a more competitive system through manufacturing, supply chain, deployment and cost decomposition rather than a single laboratory discovery.
rivalsAndFailures: Lower module price did not automatically remove soft-cost and integration bottlenecks.
Different countries reached different installed costs under different policy/market institutions.
diffusionAndScaling: Deployment and manufacturing scale interacted with cost decline, broadening the feasible market for PV.
standardsAndInstitutions: DOE/NREL/LBNL measurement, incentive programmes, utilities, manufacturers and installers occupied distinct roles.
externalitiesAndCorrections: Cost decline and deployment success do not settle land, grid, material-supply or lifecycle questions.
secondOrderEffects: As module cost fell, the relative importance of installation, permitting, finance and grid integration increased.
sourceNativeSummary: PV scale-up shows a moving bottleneck: once the core conversion technology existed, manufacturing, module price, soft costs, policy and grid/deployment interfaces increasingly determined system-level progress.
